paras.text: Bad Faith and Unfair Trade Practices: Audio Lecture

Welcome to the bad faith chapter. If you take away one thing, take this. In Michigan the words bad faith get used loosely, but the law splits the idea into three separate tools, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in this area. Fix that framework first.

Tool one is the penalty interest statute, M C L five hundred point two zero zero six. That is a private right. An insured can collect twelve percent interest on a late paid claim, no bad faith lawsuit required, just a mechanical calculation. Tool two is the unfair trade practices list, M C L five hundred point two zero two six, fourteen things an insurer is not supposed to do. The catch is that an insured cannot sue under it. It is enforced by the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, D I F S, administratively. Tool three is common law bad faith, a tort suit. Michigan does not recognize that for a first party insured suing their own carrier. It survives only when a liability insurer refuses to settle within policy limits and an excess judgment lands on its own insured. Sort everything below into one of those three buckets.

Start with tool one, section two zero zero six, the one you will use most in real claims work. Subsection one says the insurer must pay benefits on a timely basis to its insured, to a person directly entitled to benefits, or to a third party tort claimant, or in the alternative pay twelve percent interest on the late claim. Failing to do either one is an unfair trade practice, unless the claim is reasonably in dispute. Notice where that reasonably in dispute language sits. It is in subsection one, and in subsection four it protects only a narrow category of claimant. Subsection two clarifies that if the insurer loses in court and pays the judgment plus the required interest, that alone is not an additional unfair trade practice.

Subsection three is the clock everybody in claims work should have memorized. The insurer must specify in writing exactly what documents constitute a satisfactory proof of loss within thirty days after receiving the claim, unless the claim settles inside those thirty days. Once a satisfactory proof of loss is supplied, the insurer has sixty days from receiving it to pay the supported amount, or the payment is untimely. Picture a fire claim reported May first. The insurer has until roughly May thirty first to send the letter spelling out what it needs. Say the homeowner supplies everything June fifteenth. The insurer then has until roughly August fourteenth to pay the supported amount. Miss that, and subsection four is triggered.

Subsection four is the heart of the chapter, and its two sentences do very different jobs. The first says that if benefits are not paid on a timely basis, the benefits paid bear simple interest, from a date sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss was received, at the rate of twelve percent per annum, if the claimant is the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits under the insured's insurance contract. No qualifier. No mention of whether the claim was disputed. If you are the insured, or someone directly entitled to benefits under your own policy, and you get paid late, you get twelve percent.

The second sentence is where the reasonably in dispute language lives, and it applies only to third party tort claimants. For one of them to get the same twelve percent, three things must all be true. The insurer's liability must not be reasonably in dispute, the insurer must have refused payment in bad faith, and a court of law must have determined that bad faith. Much higher bar, and it belongs only to people who are not the policyholder but have a liability claim against someone the insurer covers. Four other mechanics round out subsection four. Interest is paid on top of, and at the same time as, the loss payment. If the loss exceeds the policy limit, interest runs on the limit. If the insurer offers to pay, the claimant turns it down, and never recovers more than that offer, no interest is owed. And interest under this section is offset against any separate judgment interest the insurer owes.

Now let's move to tool two, section two zero two six, the unfair trade practices list. The statute's own preamble sets the threshold, and it is worth memorizing verbatim. Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the business of insurance, other than isolated incidents, are a course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency to engage in that type of conduct. Read that closely. D I F S is looking for a pattern, not a single bad claim file. One rough denial letter, standing alone, generally will not trigger an enforcement action, though it can still be evidence somewhere else.

The list runs fourteen items, lettered a through n. The ones that come up constantly in property claims are these. Misrepresenting pertinent facts or policy provisions relating to coverage. Failing to acknowledge or act reasonably and promptly on claim communications. Failing to adopt reasonable standards for prompt investigation. Refusing to pay claims without a reasonable investigation based on the available information. Failing to affirm or deny coverage within a reasonable time after proof of loss is completed. Failing to attempt in good faith to settle promptly and fairly once liability has become reasonably clear. Compelling insureds to sue by offering substantially less than what is owed. Making a payment without stating what coverage it was paid under. Delaying investigation or payment by demanding duplicate paperwork purely to duplicate a verification already done. Failing to promptly settle one portion of a claim, where liability is clear, to pressure the insured on a different, disputed portion. And failing to give a reasonable, fact based, policy based explanation for a denial or a compromise offer. Subsection two also requires insurers to keep a complete written record of every complaint since their last D I F S exam, with the number, the type, the outcome, and the time it took. Failing to keep that record is itself a violation.

So how does D I F S enforce this list, since there is no private lawsuit? A pipeline runs through five sections. Section two zero two eight lets the commissioner investigate on probable cause. Section two zero two nine requires written notice of a hearing, but before that notice goes out, bureau staff must give the insurer a chance to confer informally, and the matter can be resolved summarily by agreement. Section two zero three zero governs the hearing. The insurer may be represented by counsel and show cause why a cease and desist order should not issue, and here is the detail that surprises people, the burden of proof sits on the agency, not the insurer. The insurer may request an independent hearing officer instead of the commissioner, and gets one dismissal of that officer within twenty days.

Section two zero three eight is where the money comes in. On a finding of violation after a hearing, the director issues written findings and a cease and desist order, and may impose a monetary penalty. For an ordinary violation, one thousand dollars per violation, capped at ten thousand total. For a knowing violation, five thousand dollars per violation, capped at fifty thousand for all violations in any six month period. The director may also suspend or revoke the license for knowing, persistent violations, and order a refund of overcharges. Section two zero four zero covers defying a cease and desist order already in effect. That runs up to twenty thousand dollars per violation, on top of suspension or revocation, and the order can never punish conduct predating it.

Now the case law, because a few of these get misquoted constantly. Start with Young versus Michigan Mutual Insurance Company, nineteen eighty four. An insured tried three theories after a denied claim, a tort claim on section two zero zero six, a tort claim on section two zero two six, and a freestanding bad faith tort. The court rejected all three. There is no implied private cause of action in tort for violation of section two zero zero six. And under section two zero two six, isolated incidents do not constitute unfair trade practices, because one insurance client's dealings with one company are, by their nature, an isolated incident. The insured does not have an independent cause of action under that section. Here is the nuance people miss. Young did not say an insured can never collect the section two zero zero six interest penalty. The same opinion notes that Michigan case law already lets a private party directly recover it. What is barred is dressing the claim up as an independent tort, not the ordinary statutory interest claim.

Next, Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company, nineteen eighty, the foundational no first party bad faith tort case. An insured sued for mental distress and exemplary damages after his disability insurer denied a claim. Here is the court's actual language, because a common paraphrase gets it wrong. The court said, we decline to follow the California court and to declare the mere bad faith breach of an insurance indemnity contract an independent and separately actionable tort. That's the real quote. You will often hear people describe Kewin's rule using the phrase wholly separate and independent duty, but that specific four word phrase is nowhere in the actual opinion. The underlying rule is the same either way, no independent tort without a duty that exists apart from the contract itself, but if you're asked to quote Kewin verbatim, use the actual words, an independent and separately actionable tort, not the borrowed phrase. Watch the outcome too. Kewin's insured kept only his contract money, sixteen thousand five hundred dollars on the disability policy plus seven hundred ninety eight dollars and forty cents on the life policy. The mental distress award stayed reversed and the fifty thousand dollar exemplary damages award was set aside. Justice Williams wrote separately and would have allowed emotional distress contract damages, but that opinion did not command the court, so do not quote it as the rule.

Now the one place Michigan does recognize bad faith as a tort, the third party duty to settle. Commercial Union Insurance Company versus Liberty Mutual Insurance Company, nineteen eighty six. It is about a liability insurer's duty to its own insured when there is a chance to settle within policy limits and an excess judgment could follow a refusal. The court defined bad faith, for jury instruction purposes, as arbitrary, reckless, indifferent, or intentional disregard of the interests of the person owed a duty. Bad faith can exist without actual dishonesty or fraud, if the insurer is motivated by protecting its own interests at the insured's expense. Honest mistakes, good faith denials, and simple negligence are not enough. The court listed twelve non exclusive factors a jury may weigh, none decisive alone, things like failing to keep the insured informed of settlement offers, failing to accept a reasonable within limits offer, ignoring the advice of an adjuster or attorney, and failing to investigate properly before refusing a settlement. And it cautioned, judge the insurer by what it knew at the time, not with twenty twenty hindsight.

Back to the first party twelve percent rule, because two cases lock it down. Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance Company, two thousand seven, a special conflict panel, held that a first party insured is entitled to twelve percent penalty interest if a claim is not timely paid, irrespective of whether the claim is reasonably in dispute. And the Michigan Supreme Court in Nickola versus M I C General Insurance Company, five hundred Michigan one fifteen, two thousand seventeen, settled it in an underinsured motorist claim. An insured claiming under their own policy cannot be treated as a third party tort claimant under subsection four, so the reasonably in dispute exemption does not reach that claim. The court called this entirely consistent with Griswold and overruled an earlier Court of Appeals case that had gone the other way.

One more correction. Smith versus Globe Life Insurance Company, nineteen ninety nine, is often cited as proof that the Michigan Consumer Protection Act does not reach insurance at all. The actual opinion says almost the opposite on its own facts. Smith actually held two things. First, and this half is still good law, the general exemption does cover the sale of insurance, because the test asks whether the general transaction is specifically authorized, not whether the specific misconduct is. Second, under the statute as it then read, the court still let the insured's consumer protection claim over a credit life policy proceed, because the exemption then in place had its own built in exception for certain private actions. The claim survived summary disposition and was remanded. The legislature closed that door shortly afterward, effective March twenty eighth, two thousand one. The current version, section four forty five point nine zero four, subsection three, says the Consumer Protection Act does not apply to, or create a cause of action for, conduct made unlawful by chapter twenty of the insurance code, for conduct occurring on or after March twenty eighth, two thousand one. So today that route really is closed for chapter twenty claims. Smith is the case that prompted the fix, not the case that states the current rule.

Finally, two things that are not law, so do not teach them as if they are. Senate Bill two forty five, from the twenty twenty five session, would add a new chapter thirty B titled the right to a civil cause of action against insurers for certain conduct. It would let a person damaged by a violation of section two zero zero six, two zero two six, or two zero two seven sue the insurer directly, with punitive and emotional distress damages if the violation was in bad faith, and a rebuttable presumption of bad faith from a two zero two six violation. In other words, it would undo Kewin and Young by statute. But as of the most recent check, it has only been reported favorably out of committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole in June of twenty twenty six. It has not passed either chamber. It is a bill, not a law. And D I F S Bulletin two thousand twenty five, dash, twenty five, dash, I N S, issued October twenty fourth of twenty twenty five, reminds insurers about improper claims administration practices, quoting the same reasonable investigation and prompt settlement subsections we covered. It is written around automobile claims, not property, so treat it as guidance, not a property rule.

Close with the numbers you need memorized. Thirty days to specify proof of loss materials. Sixty days after proof of loss to pay before interest starts. Twelve percent simple interest for the insured, no reasonably in dispute defense available to them. Fourteen enumerated unfair practices. Ten thousand dollars maximum aggregate penalty for ordinary violations, fifty thousand for knowing violations in a six month window, twenty thousand per violation for defying a cease and desist order. No first party bad faith tort. No private lawsuit under the unfair practices list. And Florida, for contrast, has a real statutory first party bad faith law. Michigan has none, only the twelve percent hammer and ordinary breach damages. Know those cold and this chapter is yours.
